quote: Lewis Carroll, who was also a mathematician, once wrote a short dialogue called “What the Tortoise said to Achilles.”
content: The lesson drawn here is the standard reading of Carroll (1895): a rule of inference can't be supplied as one more premise, so some disposition to infer must simply be exercised. Ryle (1946) gave that reading its classic form, using the regress to argue that knowing how can't be reduced to knowing that. The essay is right, and not new. Crediting that tradition would also have brought in its complications. Stanley & Williamson (2001) argue that the regress doesn't show what Ryle thought it did, and whether dispositions to reason are themselves beliefs is still an open question.

quote: There is no way to write a dynamic on a piece of paper, because the paper will just lie there.
content: Then there's no way to write one in Java either, because an applet is text until an interpreter runs it. Since von Neumann, the defining feature of general-purpose computers has been that programs are data: a general enough interpreter turns written instructions into behavior. Humans are such interpreters. People read about Bayes' theorem or long division and acquire new ways of inferring, and language models change their behavior when they read instructions. Whether something is a dynamic or just data depends on the machine reading it. That weakens the essay's later use of the distinction. An argument can't move a rock, but it can install a dynamic in any mind general enough to run it, and that is exactly the kind of mind moral arguments are addressed to.

quote: Dynamic: When the belief pool contains “X is fuzzle,” send X to the action system.
content: The fuzzle example presents the Humean theory of motivation as a fact of cognitive engineering. On that theory a belief alone can't move anyone to act without a separate desire. It is one side of a live dispute. Motivational internalists hold that sincerely judging an act right is itself a motivating state in a rational agent (Smith, The Moral Problem, 1994; Dancy, Practical Reality, 2000; books, no DOI). The essay sidesteps the dispute by using a nonsense word. "Fuzzle" is stipulated to motivate nothing, so of course believing it does nothing. Whether "right" is like "fuzzle" is the question, and the example assumes the answer.

quote: This is why you can’t argue fuzzleness into a rock.
content: No one proposed to. The minds moral philosophy addresses already perform modus ponens and already pursue goals. The question is whether such minds are rationally required to care about certain things, and the regress says nothing about that. The conclusion is correct for rocks and silent about agents, and agents are the only case at issue in the Friendly AI debate this essay sets up.
